questions.title: Statistics: Mean, Standard Deviation and Regression

subQuestions.questionText: A teacher recorded the number of hours that 10 learners spent studying for a test and the percentage mark each learner obtained. Hours studied $(x)$: 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9. Mark (%) $(y)$: 42, 48, 55, 58, 62, 68, 74, 78, 82, 88. Calculate the mean of the marks.
Calculate the standard deviation of the marks.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Use calculator (STAT mode, 1-Var Stats) on the data set
Mark 2 (A): $\sigma \approx 14{,}32$
[Population standard deviation. Accept $\sigma$ between 14,30 and 14,33.]

subQuestions.questionText: Determine how many learners scored within ONE standard deviation of the mean.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Set up interval $(\bar{x} - \sigma\,;\,\bar{x} + \sigma) = (65{,}5 - 14{,}32\,;\,65{,}5 + 14{,}32) = (51{,}18\,;\,79{,}82)$
Mark 2 (A): Marks within this interval: 55, 58, 62, 68, 74, 78. Therefore 6 learners scored within ONE standard deviation of the mean.

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of the least squares regression line in the form $\hat{y} = a + bx$. Round $a$ and $b$ to TWO decimal places.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Use calculator: STAT $\rightarrow$ CALC $\rightarrow$ LinReg(a + bx)
Mark 2 (A): $a \approx 29{,}13$
Mark 3 (A): $b \approx 6{,}61$
Final equation: $\hat{y} = 29{,}13 + 6{,}61x$

subQuestions.questionText: Use the equation in QUESTION 1.4 to predict the percentage mark of a learner who studies for 7,5 hours.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Substitute $x = 7{,}5$: $\hat{y} = 29{,}13 + 6{,}61(7{,}5) = 29{,}13 + 49{,}575 = 78{,}705$
Mark 2 (CA): Predicted mark $\approx 78{,}71\%$
[Accept any answer in the range 78,50% – 79,00% depending on rounding of $a$ and $b$.]

subQuestions.questionText: Comment on the strength and direction of the linear relationship between hours studied and marks obtained.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 ($\checkmark$): The points lie very close to a straight line that rises from left to right.
Mark 2 ($\checkmark$): There is a strong positive linear relationship between hours studied and marks obtained.
[The correlation coefficient $r \approx 0{,}996$, very close to 1, confirming a strong positive correlation.]

subQuestions.questionText: A school recorded the time (in minutes) spent on social media in one day by 80 learners. The grouped frequency table gives intervals $0 \le t < 30$ (f=8), $30 \le t < 60$ (f=14), $60 \le t < 90$ (f=24), $90 \le t < 120$ (f=18), $120 \le t < 150$ (f=10), $150 \le t < 180$ (f=6). Identify the modal class.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1 (A): $60 \le t < 90$ minutes (highest frequency = 24)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the estimated mean time spent on social media.
Draw an ogive (cumulative frequency curve) for the data on the grid provided in the ANSWER BOOK. (Refer to the ogive shown in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Plot upper boundaries vs cumulative frequency: $(0;0), (30;8), (60;22), (90;46), (120;64), (150;74), (180;80)$.
Mark 1 (M): Starting point at $(0\,;\,0)$
Mark 2 (A): All seven points correctly plotted
Mark 3 (A): Smooth ogive shape ending at $(180\,;\,80)$

subQuestions.questionText: Use the ogive to estimate the median time.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Locate cumulative frequency $= 40$ on the ogive (since $\frac{n}{2} = \frac{80}{2} = 40$). Read horizontally to the curve, then vertically down to the time axis.
Mark 2 (A): Estimated median $\approx 82$ minutes
[Accept any answer between 80 and 84 minutes when read from a hand-drawn ogive. Algebraic interpolation gives exactly 82,5 minutes.]

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the percentage of learners who spent more than 90 minutes on social media.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Number of learners spending more than 90 minutes $= 80 - 46 = 34$
Mark 2 (A): Percentage $= \frac{34}{80} \times 100\% = 42{,}5\%$

subQuestions.questionText: ABCD is a quadrilateral with vertices $A(-3\,;\,1)$, $B(1\,;\,5)$, $C(5\,;\,3)$ and $D(1\,;\,-1)$. Calculate the gradient of AB.
Determine the equation of line AB in the form $y = mx + c$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Using point $A(-3\,;\,1)$ and $m = 1$: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$
Mark 2 (A): $y - 1 = 1(x - (-3)) \Rightarrow y - 1 = x + 3$
Mark 3 (A): $y = x + 4$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the length of BC. Leave your answer in surd form.
Determine the coordinates of M, the midpoint of AC.
Show that ABCD is a parallelogram.
subQuestions.memoText:
Method: show diagonals bisect each other.
Mark 1 (M): Midpoint of AC: $M = \left(\frac{-3+5}{2}\,;\,\frac{1+3}{2}\right) = (1\,;\,2)$
Mark 2 (A): Midpoint of BD: $\left(\frac{1+1}{2}\,;\,\frac{5+(-1)}{2}\right) = (1\,;\,2)$
Mark 3 (R): Midpoint of AC = Midpoint of BD, so the diagonals bisect each other.
Mark 4 (R): $\therefore$ ABCD is a parallelogram (diagonals bisect each other).
[Alternative: show $m_{AB} = m_{DC} = 1$ AND $m_{BC} = m_{AD} = -\frac{1}{2}$, i.e. both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.]

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the size of $\hat{A}$, the angle of the parallelogram at vertex A. Round to ONE decimal place.
subQuestions.memoText:
$\hat{A}$ is the interior angle between sides AB and AD.
Mark 1 (M): $m_{AB} = 1$; $m_{AD} = \frac{1 - (-1)}{-3 - 1} = \frac{2}{-4} = -\frac{1}{2}$
Mark 2 (A): Angle of inclination of AB: $\tan\theta_1 = 1 \Rightarrow \theta_1 = 45{,}0°$. Angle of inclination of AD: $\tan\theta_2 = -\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta_2 = 180° - 26{,}565° = 153{,}435°$
Mark 3 (M): $\hat{A} = 153{,}435° - 45{,}0° = 108{,}435°$
Mark 4 (A): $\hat{A} \approx 108{,}4°$
[Alternative method using vectors / cosine rule on triangle ABD also accepted.]

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the area of parallelogram ABCD.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Area of parallelogram $= |AB| \times |AD| \times \sin A$
$|AB| = \sqrt{4^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}$; $|AD| = \sqrt{(-3-1)^2 + (1-(-1))^2} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}$
Mark 2 (M): Area $= 4\sqrt{2} \times 2\sqrt{5} \times \sin(108{,}435°) = 8\sqrt{10} \times 0{,}9487 \approx 25{,}30 \times 0{,}9487$
Mark 3 (A): Area $\approx 24$ square units
[Most efficient: shoelace formula gives Area $= \frac{1}{2}|(-3)(5-(-1)) + 1(3-1) + 5(-1-5) + 1(1-3)| = \frac{1}{2}|{-18} + 2 - 30 - 2| = \frac{1}{2}(48) = 24$.]

subQuestions.questionText: A circle has centre $M(2\,;\,-1)$ and passes through $A(-2\,;\,2)$. The line through A is a tangent to the circle at A. Determine the length of the radius MA.
Write down the equation of the circle in the form $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Standard form $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2$ with centre $M(2\,;\,-1)$ and $r = 5$
Mark 2 (A): $(x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 25$

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the gradient of MA.
Determine the equation of the tangent to the circle at A in the form $y = mx + c$.
subQuestions.memoText:
The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
Mark 1 (R): $m_{tangent} \times m_{MA} = -1$
Mark 2 (A): $m_{tangent} = -1 \div \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right) = \frac{4}{3}$
Mark 3 (M): Using $A(-2\,;\,2)$ and $m = \frac{4}{3}$: $y - 2 = \frac{4}{3}(x - (-2)) \Rightarrow y - 2 = \frac{4}{3}x + \frac{8}{3}$
Mark 4 (A): $y = \frac{4}{3}x + \frac{14}{3}$

subQuestions.questionText: K is the point diametrically opposite to A on the circle. Calculate the coordinates of K.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (R): M is the midpoint of diameter AK.
Mark 2 (M): Let $K(x\,;\,y)$. Then $\left(\frac{-2 + x}{2}\,;\,\frac{2 + y}{2}\right) = (2\,;\,-1)$
$\frac{-2+x}{2} = 2 \Rightarrow x = 6$; $\frac{2+y}{2} = -1 \Rightarrow y = -4$
Mark 3 (A): $K(6\,;\,-4)$

subQuestions.questionText: $P(7\,;\,6)$ is a point outside the circle. Calculate the length of the tangent drawn from P to the circle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Let T be the point of tangency. Then $\triangle MTP$ is right-angled at T (radius $\perp$ tangent).
Mark 1 (R): By Pythagoras: $PT^2 = MP^2 - MT^2$
Mark 2 (M): $MP^2 = (7-2)^2 + (6-(-1))^2 = 25 + 49 = 74$; $MT^2 = r^2 = 25$; $PT^2 = 74 - 25 = 49$
Mark 3 (A): $PT = 7$ units

subQuestions.questionText: Determine, with reasons, whether the point $N(5\,;\,3)$ lies inside, on or outside the circle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Calculate the distance from M to N: $MN^2 = (5-2)^2 + (3-(-1))^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16$
Mark 2 (A): $MN^2 = 25$
Mark 3 (R): Compare $MN^2$ with $r^2 = 25$: since $MN^2 = r^2$, point N lies ON the circle.
[Verify by substitution into the equation: $(5-2)^2 + (3+1)^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$ $\checkmark$]

subQuestions.questionText: Simplify the following expression to a single trigonometric ratio: $$\frac{\sin(180° + x) \cdot \cos(360° - x) \cdot \tan(180° - x)}{\cos(90° - x) \cdot \sin(-x)}$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Numerator reductions:
Mark 1 (R): $\sin(180° + x) = -\sin x$
Mark 2 (R): $\cos(360° - x) = \cos x$
Mark 3 (R): $\tan(180° - x) = -\tan x$
Numerator $= (-\sin x)(\cos x)(-\tan x) = \sin x \cdot \cos x \cdot \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \sin^2 x$
Denominator: $\cos(90° - x) = \sin x$; $\sin(-x) = -\sin x$; Denominator $= \sin x \cdot (-\sin x) = -\sin^2 x$
Mark 4 (M): Combine: $\frac{\sin^2 x}{-\sin^2 x}$
Mark 5 (A): $= -1$

subQuestions.questionText: Prove the identity: $$\frac{1 - \cos 2x}{\sin 2x} = \tan x$$
subQuestions.memoText:
LHS: $\frac{1 - \cos 2x}{\sin 2x}$
Mark 1 (R): Use identities $\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$ and $\sin 2x = 2\sin x \cos x$
Mark 2 (M): LHS $= \frac{1 - (1 - 2\sin^2 x)}{2\sin x \cos x}$
Mark 3 (A): $= \frac{2\sin^2 x}{2\sin x \cos x}$
Mark 4 (M): $= \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \tan x = $ RHS
$\therefore \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{\sin 2x} = \tan x$ (proved)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the general solution of: $\cos(2x - 30°) = \frac{1}{2}$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Reference angle: $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 60°$
Mark 2 (R): Cosine is positive in Quadrants I and IV.
Mark 3 (A): $2x - 30° = 60° + 360°k$ OR $2x - 30° = -60° + 360°k$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$
Mark 4 (A): Case 1: $2x = 90° + 360°k \Rightarrow x = 45° + 180°k$
Mark 5 (A): Case 2: $2x = -30° + 360°k \Rightarrow x = -15° + 180°k$
$x = 45° + 180°k$ OR $x = -15° + 180°k$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$

Mark 1 (M): Replace $\sin^2 x$ with $(1 - \cos^2 x)$: $2(1 - \cos^2 x) + 3\cos x - 3 = 0$
$2 - 2\cos^2 x + 3\cos x - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow -2\cos^2 x + 3\cos x - 1 = 0$
Mark 2 (A): $2\cos^2 x - 3\cos x + 1 = 0$
Mark 3 (M): Factorise: $(2\cos x - 1)(\cos x - 1) = 0$
$\therefore \cos x = \frac{1}{2}$ OR $\cos x = 1$
Mark 4 (A): $\cos x = \frac{1}{2}$: reference angle $= 60°$; cos positive in Q I and Q IV $\Rightarrow x = 60°$ or $x = 300°$
Mark 5 (A): $\cos x = 1$: $x = 0°$ or $x = 360°$
Mark 6 (A): $x = 0°,\, 60°,\, 300°,\, 360°$

subQuestions.questionText: Without using a calculator, evaluate: $\sin 75° \cdot \cos 15° - \cos 75° \cdot \sin 15°$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Recognise compound-angle identity: $\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta$
$\therefore \sin 75° \cdot \cos 15° - \cos 75° \cdot \sin 15° = \sin(75° - 15°) = \sin 60°$
Mark 2 (A): $= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

subQuestions.questionText: The graphs of $f(x) = 2\sin x$ and $g(x) = \cos(x - 30°)$ are drawn for $x \in [-180°\,;\,180°]$. Write down the amplitude of $f$.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1 (A): Amplitude $= 2$ (the coefficient of $\sin x$ in $f(x) = 2\sin x$)

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the period of $g$.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1 (A): Period $= 360°$ (since the coefficient of $x$ in $\cos(x - 30°)$ is 1)

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the values of $x$ in the interval $[-180°\,;\,180°]$ for which $f(x) = g(x)$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$2\sin x = \cos(x - 30°)$
Mark 1 (M): Expand RHS using $\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta$: $2\sin x = \cos x \cos 30° + \sin x \sin 30°$
Mark 2 (A): $2\sin x = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos x + \frac{1}{2}\sin x$
Mark 3 (A): $\frac{3}{2}\sin x = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos x$
Mark 4 (M): $\frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \Rightarrow \tan x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$
Mark 5 (A): Reference angle $= 30°$; tan positive in Q I and Q III. In $[-180°\,;\,180°]$: $x = 30°$ or $x = -150°$

subQuestions.questionText: Hence, or otherwise, determine the values of $x \in [-180°\,;\,180°]$ for which $f(x) > g(x)$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): From the graphs and intersection points found in 6.3: $f$ is above $g$ between $x = -150°$ and $x = 30°$.
Mark 2 (A): At $x = -150°$, $f = g$ (intersection); between, $f > g$; at $x = 30°$, $f = g$ (intersection)
Mark 3 (A): $-150° < x < 30°$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the maximum value of $h(x) = f(x) - 1$.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1 (A): Max $f(x) = 2$; therefore max $h(x) = 2 - 1 = 1$

subQuestions.questionText: If the graph of $g$ is shifted 30° to the LEFT to form graph $k$, write down the equation of $k$ in its simplest form.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Replace $x$ with $(x + 30°)$ in $g(x) = \cos(x - 30°)$: $k(x) = \cos((x + 30°) - 30°) = \cos x$
Mark 2 (A): $k(x) = \cos x$

subQuestions.questionText: TF is a vertical tower on horizontal ground. A and B lie on the ground at the same level as F. The angle of elevation from A to T is 35°. $AB = 50$ m, $F\hat{A}B = 70°$ and $A\hat{B}F = 60°$. Write down the size of $A\hat{F}B$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (A): In $\triangle AFB$ on the ground: $F\hat{A}B + A\hat{B}F + A\hat{F}B = 180°$ (sum of angles in a triangle)
$70° + 60° + A\hat{F}B = 180° \Rightarrow A\hat{F}B = 50°$

subQuestions.questionText: Show that $AF = \frac{50\sin 60°}{\sin 50°}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Apply the sine rule in $\triangle AFB$
Mark 2 (R): $\frac{AF}{\sin(A\hat{B}F)} = \frac{AB}{\sin(A\hat{F}B)}$
Mark 3 (A): $\frac{AF}{\sin 60°} = \frac{50}{\sin 50°} \Rightarrow AF = \frac{50\sin 60°}{\sin 50°}$ (as required)

subQuestions.questionText: Hence, calculate the height of the tower TF, correct to TWO decimal places.
subQuestions.memoText:
In right-angled $\triangle TFA$ (TF $\perp$ ground):
Mark 1 (M): $\tan 35° = \frac{TF}{AF} \Rightarrow TF = AF \cdot \tan 35°$
Mark 2 (A): $AF = \frac{50\sin 60°}{\sin 50°} = \frac{50 \times 0{,}8660}{0{,}7660} \approx 56{,}53$ m
Mark 3 (A): $TF = 56{,}53 \times \tan 35° = 56{,}53 \times 0{,}7002 \approx 39{,}58$ m

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the area of triangle AFB.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (M): Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times AB \times AF \times \sin(F\hat{A}B)$
Mark 2 (A): $= \frac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 56{,}53 \times \sin 70°$
Mark 3 (M): $= \frac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 56{,}53 \times 0{,}9397$
Mark 4 (A): Area of $\triangle AFB \approx 1\,327{,}92$ m²
[Alternative: use Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times AF \times BF \times \sin 50°$ with BF found from sine rule. Both methods give the same result.]

subQuestions.questionText: O is the centre of the circle. A, B, C, D are points on the circle. ST is a tangent to the circle at A. BD is drawn. $T\hat{A}B = 55°$ and $A\hat{B}D = 30°$. Determine, giving reasons, the size of $A\hat{D}B$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (R): $T\hat{A}B = A\hat{D}B$ (tan-chord angle)
Mark 2 (A): $\therefore A\hat{D}B = 55°$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine, giving reasons, the size of $A\hat{O}B$ (the angle subtended at the centre by chord AB on the major-arc side).
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (R): $A\hat{O}B = 2 \times A\hat{D}B$ ($\angle$ at centre $= 2 \times \angle$ at circumference, same arc AB)
Mark 2 (A): $\therefore A\hat{O}B = 2 \times 55° = 110°$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine, giving reasons, the size of $B\hat{A}D$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (R): In $\triangle ABD$: $A\hat{B}D + A\hat{D}B + B\hat{A}D = 180°$ (sum of $\angle$s in a $\triangle$)
Mark 2 (M): $30° + 55° + B\hat{A}D = 180°$
Mark 3 (A): $B\hat{A}D = 180° - 85° = 95°$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine, giving reasons, the size of $B\hat{C}D$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (R): $B\hat{A}D + B\hat{C}D = 180°$ (opp. $\angle$s of cyclic quad ABCD)
Mark 2 (A): $95° + B\hat{C}D = 180° \Rightarrow B\hat{C}D = 85°$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine, giving reasons, the size of $A\hat{O}D$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$A\hat{B}D = 30°$ subtends arc AD at the circumference.
Mark 1 (R): $A\hat{O}D = 2 \times A\hat{B}D$ ($\angle$ at centre $= 2 \times \angle$ at circumference, same arc AD)
Mark 2 (A): $\therefore A\hat{O}D = 2 \times 30° = 60°$

subQuestions.questionText: Show that $S\hat{A}D = A\hat{B}D$, giving a reason for your statement.
subQuestions.memoText:
$S\hat{A}D$ is the angle between the tangent SA and chord AD.
Mark 1 (R): By the tan-chord theorem: $S\hat{A}D$ = angle in the alternate segment = $A\hat{B}D$
Mark 2 (R): $\therefore S\hat{A}D = A\hat{B}D$ (tan-chord)

subQuestions.questionText: $\triangle PQR$ is drawn. S is on PQ and T is on PR such that $ST \parallel QR$. U is on QR such that $SU \parallel PR$. It is given that $PS:SQ = 2:3$. Prove that STRU is a parallelogram.
subQuestions.memoText:
To prove: Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
Mark 1 (R): $ST \parallel QR$ (given)
Mark 2 (M): Since U lies on QR, the segment UR is part of QR, so $ST \parallel UR$.
Mark 3 (R): $SU \parallel PR$ (given)
Mark 4 (M): Since T lies on PR, the segment TR is part of PR, so $SU \parallel TR$.
$\therefore$ STRU has both pairs of opposite sides parallel — it is a parallelogram.

subQuestions.questionText: Determine, with reasons, the value of the ratio $ST:QR$.
subQuestions.memoText:
In $\triangle PQR$ with $ST \parallel QR$:
Mark 1 (R): $\frac{PS}{PQ} = \frac{PT}{PR} = \frac{ST}{QR}$ (line parallel to one side of a triangle, or $\triangle PST ||| \triangle PQR$)
Mark 2 (M): Given $PS:SQ = 2:3$, so $\frac{PS}{PQ} = \frac{2}{2+3} = \frac{2}{5}$
Mark 3 (A): $\frac{ST}{QR} = \frac{2}{5} \Rightarrow ST:QR = 2:5$

subQuestions.questionText: Determine, with reasons, the value of the ratio $SU:PR$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Consider $\triangle QPR$. $SU \parallel PR$ with S on PQ and U on QR.
Mark 1 (M): By proportionality (or $\triangle QSU ||| \triangle QPR$)
Mark 2 (R): $\frac{QS}{QP} = \frac{SU}{PR}$
Mark 3 (A): $\frac{QS}{QP} = \frac{3}{2+3} = \frac{3}{5}$, so $\frac{SU}{PR} = \frac{3}{5} \Rightarrow SU:PR = 3:5$

subQuestions.questionText: Prove that $\triangle PST ||| \triangle PQR$.
subQuestions.memoText:
In $\triangle PST$ and $\triangle PQR$:
Mark 1 (R): $P\hat{S}T = P\hat{Q}R$ (corresponding $\angle$s, $ST \parallel QR$)
Mark 2 (R): $P\hat{T}S = P\hat{R}Q$ (corresponding $\angle$s, $ST \parallel QR$)
Mark 3 (R): $\hat{P}$ is common.
Mark 4 (R): $\therefore \triangle PST ||| \triangle PQR$ (AAA)

subQuestions.questionText: Hence, determine the ratio area $\triangle PST$ : area $\triangle PQR$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (R): If two triangles are similar, the ratio of their areas equals the square of the ratio of corresponding sides.
Mark 2 (M): From 9.2: $\frac{ST}{QR} = \frac{2}{5}$
Mark 3 (M): $\frac{\text{area}(\triangle PST)}{\text{area}(\triangle PQR)} = \left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2$
Mark 4 (A): $= \frac{4}{25}$
$\therefore$ area $\triangle PST$ : area $\triangle PQR = 4:25$
